title: Lesson 15: Special Division
subtopics: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
learningGoals: Perform special division mentally by using the divisor's relation to a nearby base.
Track running quotient digits, carries, and remainder adjustments without losing place value.
Check special-division answers by rebuilding the dividend from divisor times quotient plus remainder.
coreIdeas: Special division is driven by the divisor's deficiency from or excess over a base such as 10 or 100.
The board layout matters: the base decides the remainder split, and the flagged digits control the running corrections.
A correct special-division answer should always rebuild the dividend when checked.

workedExamples.method: This gives the remainder in 23 ÷ 9 after the first quotient digit 2 is brought down.
This gives the second answer block in 121314 ÷ 99 after bringing down 12.
This gives the remainder in 235 ÷ 88 after multiplying the deficiency 12 by the quotient 2.
This rebuilds the dividend in the check for 1489 ÷ 123 = 12 remainder 13.

starterPractice: Warm-up: divide 23 by 9 by naming the quotient digit and the digit-sum remainder.
Guided: divide 121314 by 99 by working in pairs of digits.
Independent: check 1489 ÷ 123 by rebuilding the dividend from quotient and remainder.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting Special Division.
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 15: confident. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Perform special division mentally by using the divisor's relation to a nearby base.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in Special Division with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.
A quick review prompt decides whether the learner advances or repeats.

rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak visible on every step and protect it with immediate retries instead of long explanations.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each exercise group has one badge focus tied to the subtopic being learned.

reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Use the micro-practice line as the first repair loop before advancing.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the learner can answer the checkpoint and complete one try in the same subtopic.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise A: Division by 9 for short numbers
sessionFlow.coachHook: For division by 9, the first digit becomes the first quotient digit, and the sum of the digits gives the remainder, with an extra adjustment if the remainder still contains another 9.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 23 ÷ 9, 66 ÷ 9, and 58 ÷ 9, then show first-digit quotient and digit-sum remainder on the board.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Division by 9 for short numbers is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The first digit is the starting quotient.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find 51 ÷ 9 and 66 ÷ 9 by saying the first quotient and the first remainder before adjusting.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise B: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
sessionFlow.coachHook: For longer numbers divided by 9, each quotient digit is added to the next dividend digit to build the next quotient digit, and a short cut prevents double figures from piling up.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 2301 ÷ 9 and 3172 ÷ 9 left to right, first in the full carry style and then with the short cut.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9 is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The first digit is still brought down directly.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Divide 2301 by 9 and 777 by 9 by speaking each running total before the next digit is written.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise C: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
sessionFlow.coachHook: For a divisor below 10, use the gap from 10: double for 8, treble for 7, and so on, adding that multiple of the current quotient digit to the next dividend digit.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 31 ÷ 8, 211 ÷ 8, and 123 ÷ 7, then mark the deficiency from 10 beside each divisor.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10 is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The deficiency tells you the multiplier.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find 31 ÷ 8 and 123 ÷ 7 by naming the deficiency multiplier before the remainder step.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise D: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
sessionFlow.coachHook: For divisors near 100, split the dividend into pairs, bring the first pair down, and use either direct addition for 99 or doubled additions for 98 as you move along.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 121314 ÷ 99 and 121314 ÷ 98 with the dividend split into pairs and the working written two digits at a time.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100 is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The base determines the block size.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Work 121314 ÷ 99 and 121314 ÷ 98 by saying each pair you write down before the remainder.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise E: Divisor below a base number
sessionFlow.coachHook: When the divisor is just below a base like 100 or 10000, flag its deficiency from the base, bring down the leading answer digits, and add the flagged products into the remainder columns.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 235 ÷ 88 and 31313 ÷ 7887 with the base deficiency written underneath the divisor and the vertical line marking the remainder part.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Divisor below a base number is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The base tells you where the remainder begins.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Use the flagged deficiency method on 235 ÷ 88 and 31313 ÷ 7887, then check by multiplication plus remainder.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise F: Divisor above a base number
sessionFlow.coachHook: A divisor just above the base uses the same layout as the below-base method, but the flagged part is treated as negative, so the running products are subtracted rather than added.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 1489 ÷ 123 and 2211 ÷ 112 with barred flag digits to show that the corrections are subtractive.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Divisor above a base number is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: This is transpose and apply in a division setting.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Use the above-base method on 1489 ÷ 123 and then rebuild the dividend to check the answer.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 9 for short numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Nine is one less than ten, so division by nine creates a very short pattern.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 23 ÷ 9 with the 2 and 3 separated.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The first digit is the starting quotient.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 9 for short numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: In twenty-three divided by nine, the first digit two is the quotient and two plus three gives the remainder five.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 2 as quotient and 2 + 3 = 5 as remainder.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
screenplay.fallbackHint: So 23 ÷ 9 is 2 remainder 5.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 9 for short numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: If the remainder still contains another nine, as in sixty-six divided by nine, adjust again: six remainder twelve becomes seven remainder three.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 6 + 6 = 12, then 12 - 9 = 3 and increase the quotient by 1.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
screenplay.fallbackHint: A remainder bigger than 8 must be adjusted.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 9 for short numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Now do fifty-eight divided by nine using the same adjustment idea.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 5 + 8 = __ and then subtract one extra nine.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The first remainder is 13, then one more nine fits.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 9 for short numbers
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what is the one warning sign that tells you to adjust the answer after the first remainder?
screenplay.boardAction: Box the phrase remainder still contains a 9.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 9 turn the first digit into the quotient and the digit sum into the remainder?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: If the remainder is 9 or more, add one to the quotient and reduce the remainder by 9.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That adjustment completes the rule.

screenplay.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
screenplay.teacherLine: A longer dividend keeps passing information forward from one digit to the next.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 2301 ÷ 9 with space for three quotient digits and a remainder.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The first digit is still brought down directly.

screenplay.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
screenplay.teacherLine: Bring down the 2, then add 2 to the next digit 3 to make 5, then add 5 to 0 to make 5, and finally add 5 to 1 to get remainder 6.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 2, 5, 5 and remainder 6 in order.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Each quotient digit feeds the next step.

screenplay.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
screenplay.teacherLine: In 3172 ÷ 9 a double figure appears, so the short cut carries early: 3, then 4, then 11 becomes 5 with the 1 carried, giving 352 remainder 4.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the shortcut version beneath the full version.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Early carrying prevents large quotient digits.

screenplay.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
screenplay.teacherLine: Now try seven hundred seventy-seven divided by nine with the short cut.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 7, then the next total 14, then the next total 15 with blanks.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Carry before the double figure grows further.

screenplay.subtopic: Longer numbers and shortcut carries in division by 9
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what is the short-cut principle when a two-digit number appears in the quotient-building process?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave carry early written beside the example.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does each quotient digit create the next one in longer division by 9?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Carry the extra ten immediately into the previous answer digit.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That keeps the running answer tidy.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
screenplay.teacherLine: A divisor like 8 or 7 is treated by how far it sits below 10.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 8 as 10 - 2 and 7 as 10 - 3.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The deficiency tells you the multiplier.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
screenplay.teacherLine: For thirty-one divided by eight, bring down 3, double it to 6, add the last digit 1, and get remainder 7.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 6 + 1 = 7 beside 31 ÷ 8.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Because 8 is 2 below 10, we double.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
screenplay.teacherLine: For one hundred twenty-three divided by seven, bring down 1, treble it to 3, add 2 to make 5, then treble 5 to 15 and add 3 to make 18, which adjusts to 17 remainder 4.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the trebling chain and the final adjustment.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Because 7 is 3 below 10, we treble.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
screenplay.teacherLine: Now do 211 ÷ 8 by doubling the running quotient digit at each step.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 4 + 1 = __ and then 10 + 1 = __.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The first running quotient is 5, then the remainder adjusts from 11.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 8, 7, and similar divisors below 10
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what number do you multiply by at each step when the divisor is below 10?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave deficiency from 10 boxed.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does division by 8 use doubles and division by 7 use triples?
screenplay.fallbackHint: That deficiency controls the whole method.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
screenplay.teacherLine: A base of 100 means the work moves in two-digit blocks instead of one-digit blocks.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 12 / 13 / 14 under 99 and 98.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The base determines the block size.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
screenplay.teacherLine: For division by 99, bring down 12, then add 12 to 13 to get 25, and then add 25 to 14 to get remainder 39.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 12 / 25 remainder 39.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Division by 99 behaves like division by 9 but in pairs.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
screenplay.teacherLine: For division by 98, the divisor is 2 below 100, so double the last answer block before adding: 2 x 12 + 13 = 37, then 2 x 37 + 14 = 88.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 12 / 37 remainder 88.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The deficiency from 100 drives the step.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
screenplay.teacherLine: Now say the next pair when 12 has already come down in 121314 ÷ 98.
screenplay.boardAction: Leave 2 x 12 + 13 = __ blank.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Double the last answer block and add the next pair.

screenplay.subtopic: Division by 99, 98, and similar divisors near 100
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what decides whether you simply add the next pair or double before adding it?
screenplay.boardAction: Box 99 is 1 below 100 and 98 is 2 below 100.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do we work in pairs of digits when dividing by 99 or 98?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: The deficiency of the divisor from 100.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That is the pairwise version of the earlier rule.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor below a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: A divisor below a base behaves like a whole base minus a deficiency.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 88 as 100 - 12 and mark the remainder split two digits from the right.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The base tells you where the remainder begins.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor below a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: In 235 ÷ 88, bring down 2 into the answer, multiply the deficiency 12 by 2 to get 24, and add that to 35 to get remainder 59.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 24 + 35 = 59 beneath the dividend.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The deficiency products accumulate into the remainder.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor below a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: For 31313 ÷ 7887, the deficiency is 2113, so 3 x 2113 = 6339, and adding that into the last four columns gives remainder 7652.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 2113 x 3 = 6339 and the final remainder build.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Larger bases use larger flagged deficiencies.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor below a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: Now check the first example by rebuilding the dividend from quotient and remainder.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: A correct quotient-remainder pair rebuilds the dividend.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor below a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what two things does the base number tell you in this method?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave deficiency and vertical split marked on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the flagged deficiency create the remainder when the divisor is below the base?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: It tells you the flagged deficiency and where the remainder columns begin.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Those are the board anchors for the method.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor above a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: A divisor above a base means the correction must subtract from the later columns, not add to them.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 123 as 100 + 23 and show flagged bar digits 2 and 3.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This is transpose and apply in a division setting.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor above a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: For 1489 ÷ 123, bring down 1, subtract the flagged 23 from the following columns to produce the next quotient digit 2, then subtract 46 to reach remainder 13.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 4 - 2 = 2, 8 - 4 = 4, 9 - 6 = 3 with the final remainder 13.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The corrections are negative because the divisor is above the base.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor above a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: A negative-looking remainder or quotient adjustment can still be repaired at the end, as in 2211 ÷ 112 where the first answer must be lowered and the remainder increased.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the final adjustment from 20 remainder -29 to 19 remainder 83.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Final adjustment keeps the quotient and remainder valid.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor above a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: Now check 1489 ÷ 123 by rebuilding the dividend.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Quotient times divisor plus remainder must recover the dividend.

screenplay.subtopic: Divisor above a base number
screenplay.teacherLine: Final checkpoint: what is the sign difference between the below-base and above-base division methods?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave add flagged products and subtract flagged products side by side.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do the flagged digits become negative when the divisor is above the base?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Below-base uses positive flagged products, above-base uses negative flagged products.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That sign choice separates the two methods.

teachingFlowStages.intent: Introduce special division as base-driven correction rather than long division repetition.
Explain the running addition, deficiency multiplication, and flagged correction patterns for each divisor type.
Demonstrate short and long division by 9, below-10 divisors, pairwise base-100 divisors, and base-adjacent divisors.
Have the learner predict the next quotient or remainder block before it is written.
Mix one-digit, pairwise, below-base, and above-base examples so the learner chooses the correct division variant.
Use dividend rebuild checks to confirm quotient and remainder are both correct.
Require the learner to explain how the sign and size of the flagged correction change with the divisor.
